Unlike in 'movie-thermodynamics' (the movie 'Sunshine' being a recent example) where the astronaut exposed to the vacuum of space in the shadow of the ship freezes into an icecube in 10 seconds, the heat loss in space isn't instantaneous or even a quick process. It's cold, but you don't lose heat that fast because there is no convective loss of heat or conductive loss of heat, only loss of heat through thermal radiation.

As an example, you can stick your arm or hand inside a convection oven, heated to 450 and the air won't burn you if you're in there for 5 seconds because the heat transfer from the relatively motionless air to skin isn't high.

Don't try putting your hand or arm in a liquid heated to 450 because you'll get 3rd degree burns in less than a second, due to the high rate of heat transfer between the liquid and your skin.

In space, the rate of heat transfer is very very low, so heat doesn't flow away from items very quickly.

But if you were permanently in the shadow (of a planet, moon, structure) or if there was not any rotation to even out the heating, then the side in the shade would drift towards the low temperature of space (and contract), and the hot side would get hotter and hotter (and expand).

Also if the rotation were so slow that the shade side could fully dissipate the heat before it came into the sun again, then your theory would be correct and it would be under constant expansion and contraction.
